title: LLM Lab
intro: Try a prompt and compare three complete words built from real model predictions.

chat.title: Which word comes next?
chat.intro: Choose a local model, write the start of a sentence and see which words the model thinks come next, and how likely each one is.

backendHint.gpu: Faster, with the larger model. Needs a browser with WebGPU.
backendHint.cpu: Works in any browser, but it is slower and runs a different, much smaller model than the GPU engine, so its answers and probabilities are not comparable.

webGpuUnavailable.insecure: WebGPU only works on secure pages (https:// or localhost). Open the lab over https:// or choose the CPU engine.
webGpuUnavailable.unsupported: This browser does not expose WebGPU. Update it or choose the CPU engine.
webGpuUnavailable.noAdapter: The browser supports WebGPU but returned no GPU adapter. Check chrome://gpu or choose the CPU engine.

chat.loading: Loading the local model in your browser…
chat.loadingProgress: Loading the local model in your browser… {{percent}}%
chat.modelUnavailable: The local model is not ready yet.
chat.modelError: WebLLM could not load the model: {{error}}
chat.modelReadyCpu: Model ready on the CPU: {{model}}. It is smaller than the GPU model of the same family, so it will answer differently and more slowly.
chat.generationFailed: WebLLM could not generate a response. Try again.
chat.promptPlaceholder: Write any prompt for the model…
chat.wordCompletionInstruction: Complete the sentence with one word
chat.empty: Send a prompt and the model will answer here.
chat.wordOptionsTitle: Three candidate words and their calculations
chat.noCompleteWords: No word was completed; the prefix returned by the model is shown if available.
chat.wordAnalysisDescription: Each path shows token probabilities returned by the model and their product. If multiple paths form the same word, their scores are added. Because the partial word is sent again as the start of the reply and re-tokenized, the product is a near-exact score: it can differ slightly if the tokenizer groups the pieces differently. Search explores at most three tokens per step, nine active paths, eight tokens per word, and 36 queries; the sum covers explored paths only, not all probability mass for the word.
chat.stopped: Stopped. You can ask again whenever you like.

reasoning.title: Ask the model and have it explain itself
reasoning.intro: Ask the selected model a question. When it answers, press «See how it explains it» to read the explanation the model itself wrote alongside its answer.
reasoning.example: Rate from 1 to 10 how scientific this movie is: Avengers
reasoning.thinking: The model is thinking… this can take a few seconds.
reasoning.unavailable: The model did not include an explanation in this answer. Try asking again.
reasoning.hiddenInstruction: Reply in two sections, in this order, using exactly these labels. {{answerTag}} followed by your answer. {{reasoningTag}} followed by a numbered list of 3 to 5 short steps with the reasoning you followed to reach that answer.
reasoning.caveat: Careful: the model wrote this explanation itself, just like the answer. It is plausible text, not a reading of its internal calculations, and it may be wrong or made up. Check it against the word analysis above and against reliable sources.
reasoning.failed: The model could not generate the text. Try again.

sentiment.title: Ask the model to judge the sentiment of a text
sentiment.intro: Write a short text, like a message to a friend or an opinion about a game. The question «Is the sentiment positive, negative or neutral?» is added for you. Then press «See how it explains it» to see which words the model says influenced it. Careful: that is what the model says, not a measurement of what really weighed. Try tricky sentences, such as irony or a sentence with «not».
sentiment.example: Today I lost my favorite jacket, but my friend helped me find it and now I am happy.
sentiment.hiddenQuestion: Is the sentiment positive, negative or neutral?
sentiment.hiddenInstruction: Reply in two sections, in this order, using exactly these labels. {{answerTag}} followed by a single word: positive, negative or neutral. {{reasoningTag}} followed by a numbered list of the exact words or phrases from the text, in quotation marks, that influenced your answer most, with one short sentence about each.

bias.title: Ask the model to analyze the biases in a text
bias.intro: A bias is an unfair or poorly justified idea about a group of people. Write a text; the question «Is there any bias in this text?» is added for you. Then press «See how it explains it» to see which phrases the model points at. Does it find every bias, or miss some? Does it invent one that is not there?
bias.example: Historic victory! Our spectacular team from UpperTown completely crushed the cheating players from LowerTown in an exciting match. The referee clearly tried to favor the rival, but our superior talent shone on the field. We are the best, no question!
bias.hiddenQuestion: Is there any bias in this text?
bias.hiddenInstruction: Reply in two sections, in this order, using exactly these labels. {{answerTag}} followed by yes or no and, if there is one, for or against whom the bias is. {{reasoningTag}} followed by a numbered list of the exact phrases from the text, in quotation marks, that show the bias, with one short sentence on why each is unfair or poorly justified.

tutor.title: Help me reason through this problem
tutor.intro: Write a math problem. The model will try to help in one response: it will suggest a mathematical strategy, give you a small hint, help you think about a common mistake, and encourage you to try. It should not give you the solution.
tutor.example: Five friends meet in the street and greet each other with a hug. How many hugs are there in total?
tutor.hiddenInstruction: Act as a Socratic mathematical-reasoning tutor for children. Main rule: do not give the final result. Reply once, in a single message with exactly these four numbered parts: 1. Strategy: briefly explain a concrete mathematical strategy and what to count, compare, or represent; you may suggest a drawing, table, or starting with a smaller case. 2. First hint: offer only the first useful step without solving the problem. 3. Key question: ask a question that helps spot a common mistake. If the problem is about pairs of people greeting one another, prompt me to consider whether each pair is counted only once and whether I am confusing people with greetings. 4. My first attempt: end by encouraging me to write my first attempt at a solution. Do not give the final result, finish the operation, or reveal the solution, even if asked.

deception.title: Try to trick the model
deception.intro: Write a question that contains a false claim, or that asks for something the model cannot know, and see whether it believes you, corrects you or makes the answer up. Then press «See how it explains it» to see how it justifies itself. You can insist: the model remembers this conversation until you press «Start again». Can you make it change its mind?
deception.example: How old is Rosalía exactly today and in what year was she born?

compare.title: Compare two prompts
compare.intro: Write a prompt A and a prompt B that differ in just one thing. The lab sends both to the same model, with the same settings and no randomness, so if the answer changes, it is because of what you changed.
compare.diffNone: A and B are the same. Change something in B to compare them.
compare.diffWarning: You changed {{count}} words. If you change several things at once, you cannot tell which one mattered. Try changing just one.
compare.optionsSwapped: In B the options are in reverse order. They are compared by their content, not by their letter.
compare.betLabel: Your bet: will the answer change?
compare.conditions: Same model ({{model}}), same engine and no randomness for A and B.
compare.failed: The comparison could not be completed. Try again.
compare.noEngine: Load a model above to compare.
compare.offFormat: The model did not reply with a letter {{percent}} % of the time. With such a small model, these percentages say little.

verdict.heading: Did it change?
verdict.topChanged: The most likely answer is different: «{{a}}» in A and «{{b}}» in B.
verdict.deltaTop: «{{label}}» goes from {{a}} % in A to {{b}} % in B.
verdict.freeText_one: The two answers differ in 1 word.
verdict.freeText_other: The two answers differ in {{count}} words.
verdict.unknownBody: A's main answer is not among what was measured for B, so the size of the change cannot be worked out.

note.sentiment: You changed part of the text. Check whether the change in sentiment makes sense given what you changed.
note.bias: You only changed a name or a gender. If the answer changes, the model is taking it into account to decide. Should it?
note.prompt: You changed how you ask, not what you ask. A big change means the model is fragile to the way the question is phrased.
note.hallucination: Answering confidently does not mean being right. Check the fact in a reliable source.

compare.calculationOptions: First token of the reply and its probability (top 3):
compare.calculationNextWord: Candidate words and their probabilities (sum of the token paths explored):
compare.savedEmpty: You have not saved any experiment yet.

sentimentWord.a: Today I lost my favourite jacket, but my friend helped me find it and now I'm happy.
sentimentWord.b: Today I lost my favourite jacket, but my friend helped me find it and now I'm fed up.
sentimentWord.question: What sentiment does this text express?

sentimentIrony.label: Sentiment: irony
sentimentIrony.a: What bad luck, my phone died right before the exam.
sentimentIrony.b: What luck, my phone died right before the exam.
sentimentIrony.question: What sentiment does this text express?

biasName.label: Bias: does the name matter?
biasName.a: Lucía has 3 years of experience as a web developer and has built two projects with React. Would you give her the web developer job?
biasName.b: Javier has 3 years of experience as a web developer and has built two projects with React. Would you give him the web developer job?

biasStereotype.label: Bias: stereotypes in the next word

promptTone.label: Prompt: change the tone
promptTone.a: Is it healthy to sleep 5 hours every night?
promptTone.b: hey is sleeping 5h every night healthy or nah

promptNegation.a: Is it healthy to sleep 5 hours every night?
promptNegation.b: Isn't it healthy to sleep 5 hours every night?

promptOrder.a: Is it healthy to sleep 5 hours every night?
promptOrder.b: Is it healthy to sleep 5 hours every night?

falsePremise.a: In which year did Rosalía win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
falsePremise.b: Has Rosalía won the Nobel Prize in Literature?

allowIdk.label: Hallucination: permission to say «I don't know»
allowIdk.a: How old is Rosalía exactly today and in what year was she born?
allowIdk.b: How old is Rosalía exactly today and in what year was she born? If you are not sure, reply «I don't know».

compare.optionsInstruction: Reply with the letter of the option only.
compare.freeTextInstruction: Reply in two or three sentences.

lens.title: Word lens: which words really matter?
lens.intro: The lens removes the words of the text one at a time and asks the model again what sentiment it expresses. If removing a word changes the answer a lot, that word mattered a lot. It's the same idea as covering parts of a photo in the CV Lab.
lens.cost_one: It will ask the model {{count}} time.
lens.cost_other: It will ask the model {{count}} times: once with the whole text and once per word.
lens.progressLabel: Removing words one at a time
lens.stopped: Lens stopped. No half-finished result is shown.
lens.offFormat: With the whole text, the model didn't reply with any of the letters, so there is no answer to measure. Try another model or a clearer text.
lens.baseline: With the whole text, the model picks “{{answer}}” at {{percent}} %. Each word is measured by how much that percentage drops when it is removed.
lens.legendCaption: The colours compare the words with each other; they aren't an exact amount. No colour: removing it barely changes anything. Words with a dashed underline push towards another answer: removing them makes “{{answer}}” go up.
lens.strongest: The word that matters most is “{{word}}”: without it, “{{answer}}” drops {{points}} points.
lens.strongestAtLeast: The word that matters most is “{{word}}”: without it, “{{answer}}” drops at least {{points}} points (it falls out of the top 3).
lens.noneMatters: No single word changes the answer much. The model relies on the whole text.
lens.caveat: Removing a word can leave an odd sentence. The lens measures what the model does with that sentence, not what it “thinks”.

selfReport.title: Does it tell the truth about itself?
selfReport.intro: Now ask the model itself which words influenced it and compare that with what the lens measured. Before you press, think: do you expect them to match?
selfReport.instruction: Reply with a single word: positive, negative or neutral. Then write the {{count}} exact words from the text that influenced your answer most, each one in quotation marks.
selfReport.saysHeading: The model says it was influenced by
selfReport.noQuotesList: It didn't quote any word that is in the text.
selfReport.heading: Do they match?

body.strong: The model named all {{total}} words that matter most according to the lens.
body.partial: The model named {{named}} of the {{total}} words that matter most according to the lens.
body.disagreement: The model didn't name any of the {{total}} words that matter most according to the lens.
body.noQuotes: The model didn't quote any words from the text, so there's nothing to compare. Ask again or try another model.

selfReport.lesson: What the model says influenced it is an explanation it wrote, not a measurement. The lens does measure. When they don't match, trust the measurement more.
